nameStory: Redroot amaranth gets its name from its distinctive taproot, which reveals a bright reddish or pinkish color when you pull up the plant. The word 'amaranth' comes from the Greek meaning 'unfading flower,' referring to how the dried flower clusters keep their color and shape long after the plant dies. It's also called 'pigweed' because farmers traditionally fed it to their pigs, though this humble weed is actually quite nutritious!
description: Redroot amaranth is a sturdy annual weed that can grow anywhere from 1 to 6 feet tall, with a bushy, upright shape. It has simple oval leaves and produces dense, greenish flower clusters that look almost fuzzy or bristly at the tips of branches. The whole plant has a somewhat coarse, rough appearance and feels sturdy to the touch. You'll often find it growing in disturbed soil, gardens, and farm fields throughout New England.

idTips.label: Root
idTips.description: Pull up a small plant to reveal the telltale reddish or pink taproot that gives this species its name - it's like nature's own red marker

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, bristly clusters of tiny greenish flowers at branch tips that feel rough and scratchy when you brush against them, almost like a bottle brush

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to diamond-shaped leaves that alternate up the stem, feeling slightly fuzzy or velvety to the touch with prominent veins underneath

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright plant with multiple branches that feels substantial and coarse, not delicate - you can't easily break the stem with your fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, shiny black seeds that fall easily from mature flower clusters when shaken, making a soft rattling sound

habitat: You'll find redroot amaranth thriving in disturbed, nitrogen-rich soils like gardens, farm fields, vacant lots, and roadsides throughout New England. It loves sunny spots with loose, cultivated soil and is especially common where fertilizers have been used. This adaptable weed can handle poor conditions but really takes off in rich garden soil.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic reddish taproot already visible if you gently dig around the base.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and produce their bristly flower clusters from mid to late summer, looking most robust and identifiable during this peak growing season.
seasonality.fall: Flower clusters turn brown and release seeds, while the whole plant may take on reddish tints before dying back with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist as dried skeletons, and seeds remain viable in the soil, ready to sprout when warm weather returns.

funFact: This humble 'weed' is actually a nutritional powerhouse - its leaves contain more protein than many common vegetables and are packed with vitamins A and C, making it a valuable wild edible that's been feeding people for thousands of years!
confusionNotes: Redroot amaranth is easily confused with other pigweeds in the amaranth family, but the reddish taproot is your best identifying feature. If you can't dig up the root, look for the dense, bristly flower clusters that feel scratchy - they're more compact and bottle-brush-like than the looser, drooping clusters of some relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'pigweed' fool you into thinking this plant is worthless - it's actually one of the most nutritious wild edibles you can find. However, be cautious about eating plants from areas where heavy fertilizers have been used, as amaranths can concentrate nitrates in their leaves to potentially harmful levels.
compareHints: Among New England amaranths, redroot is distinguished by its reddish taproot and compact, bristly flower clusters. Smooth pigweed has similar growth but lacks the red root, while love-lies-bleeding has distinctive drooping, rope-like flower clusters. Palmer's amaranth (mostly southern) has longer, more pointed leaves and different flower arrangements.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the weedy Redroot Amaranth found in gardens and fields, Tidalmarsh Amaranth is strictly a coastal specialist that grows much taller and in dense colonies.

Purple amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives by its distinctly prostrate, mat-forming growth habit - while redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed grow upright like small bushes, purple amaranth sprawls along the ground.
Among its amaranth relatives, red amaranth stands out for its particularly robust, upright growth and thick, erect flower spikes.
Love-lies-bleeding stands out dramatically from its wild amaranth relatives in New England because of its long, pendulous flower clusters - all the others have upright, spike-like flower heads.
Compared to redroot amaranth, smooth pigweed has less hairy stems and leaves, and its flower spikes tend to be more upright rather than drooping.
Among the New England amaranths, rough-fruit amaranth stands out for its preference for wetter habitats and its distinctively bumpy seeds.
Among New England's amaranths, green amaranth is unique for maintaining its green color throughout the season - most others develop reddish or purplish tones in stems, roots, or flower clusters.
Among New England's amaranths, spiny amaranth is the only one with actual spines - species like redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed may have bristly flowers but lack the sharp spines at leaf bases.
Palmer's Amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives because it's 'dioecious' - meaning individual plants are either male or female, not both like most other amaranths.
Powell's amaranth differs from redroot amaranth by lacking the red-tinged roots and having less hairy leaves.
Unlike its weedy cousins like Redroot Amaranth that grow tall and upright in disturbed soils, Seabeach Amaranth stays flat against the sand and has much thicker, more succulent leaves and stems.
